identification.summary: TeamSpy is a cyber-espionage operation publicized in March 2013 and named for its abuse of the legitimate TeamViewer remote access tool [S1]. CrySyS Lab (Budapest) began investigating after Hungary's National Security Authority reported an ongoing high-profile targeted attack in Hungary, and found the compromise was not isolated [S4]. Kaspersky published a parallel analysis the same month [S1].
identification.firstObserved: NBC News, citing the CrySyS report, said the first infections traced to 2010 and that distinct campaigns numbered in the order of tens [S6]. Press coverage described the operation as possibly a decade old [S4].
identification.notes: Primary names in this record: TeamSpy Crew (also Anger Bear and Team Bear per CrowdStrike, IRON LYRIC per Secureworks CTU, as imported from MISP Galaxy; these alias attributions were not independently confirmed in the sources gathered). Kaspersky noted similarities to the separate Red October campaign but found no direct link [S1][S5]. Original Kaspersky pages could not be fetched in this session; claims rest on search-result excerpts of those pages and on press coverage.

attribution.confidence: Kaspersky said it found strong evidence in the malware components and C2 infrastructure that the operators are Russian speakers [S1][S5]. No source gathered attributes the activity to a state sponsor.
attribution.basis: Kaspersky language and infrastructure indicators, and Russian-term and keyword similarities to Red October, with no direct link to Red October established [S1][S5].

objectives: Information theft: the toolkit searched for documents with names tied to 'secret' and 'password' [S3]. Experts quoted in press coverage said it was not entirely clear what data the attackers sought, though they had specific targets in mind [S4].

targeting.notes: Kaspersky described the operation as targeting high-level political and human rights activists across the CIS and Eastern Europe [S1]. CrySyS found different campaigns targeted different regions, and later campaigns reached users in Europe, the Middle East, Africa, North America and Asia [S6]. A press report described government, research and heavy-industry targets [S3][S6].

capabilities.summary: The crew installed a legitimate copy of TeamViewer on victim machines and modified it via DLL hijacking (a module named Avicap32) to run silently and give remote access, with a basic HTTP bot added [S3][S1]. Reported functions include desktop access, webcam or microphone activation and file transfer [S1][S3]. Initial access relied on watering-hole sites and exploit kits using two older vulnerabilities, CVE-2010-0188 (Adobe Reader/Acrobat) and CVE-2012-0507 (Oracle Java) [S1]. Kaspersky judged the tools far less sophisticated and professional than Red October's [S1][S5].

campaigns.name: Earliest traced infections
campaigns.summary: NBC News, citing the CrySyS report, said the first TeamSpy infections traced to 2010, with distinct campaigns in the order of tens [S6].

campaigns.name: Hungarian high-profile target and public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Hungary's National Security Authority alerted CrySyS to an ongoing attack on a high-profile Hungarian governmental target; CrySyS published its report in March 2013 and Kaspersky published its own analysis [S4][S1].

diamond.adversary: Operators assessed by Kaspersky as Russian speakers; sponsor unknown [S1].
diamond.capability: TeamViewer abuse with DLL hijacking (Avicap32), HTTP bot, watering holes and exploit kits using CVE-2010-0188 and CVE-2012-0507 [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-controlled C2 containing Russian-language indicators per Kaspersky [S1]; further details not captured in sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Government, industry, research bodies and activists, mainly Eastern Europe and the CIS, later wider [S1][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Purpose unclear; interest in 'secret' and 'password' documents, and in activists and government bodies [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints with unpatched Adobe Reader and Java, and legitimate remote-access software that blends into normal traffic [S1].

gaps: Kaspersky Securelist, Dark Reading and Malpedia pages could not be fetched (network resolution failure); details come from search excerpts and press coverage, so IOCs, victim counts and C2 details were not verified.
No sponsor or government attribution is available; only Russian-language indicators from Kaspersky [S1].

Alias mapping (Anger Bear, Team Bear, IRON LYRIC) comes from imported MISP Galaxy data; no cited Secureworks or CrowdStrike page was seen. The Secureworks URL in the record covers IRON LIBERTY, a different group.
No reporting after 2013 was found; current status of the activity is unknown.
Red October overlap was noted by Kaspersky only as similarity, with no direct link [S1].
The CrySyS report URL could not be confirmed in search results and was removed; CrySyS-derived details (e.g. .pgp/.p12 file searches) were dropped.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Endpoints with remote-access tools and workstations of government staff and activists are key terrain [S1]. STEP 2: Adversary reliance on legitimate software and old CVEs means weak patch hygiene is the exploitable condition [S1]. STEP 3: Template is watering hole or exploit kit, then trojanized TeamViewer with DLL hijacking, then document collection [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-sophistication, long-dwell collection against government and political targets in Europe and the CIS. MDCOA is use of legitimate remote-access tooling at scale against coalition personnel to evade signature detection. Candidate indicators: unauthorized TeamViewer installs, avicap32.dll loaded from non-system paths [S1]. Evidence is dated 2013; confirm current relevance.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: application allow-listing and inventory of remote-access software should feed common operating picture. (2) Authorities: removal of unsanctioned remote tools needs system-owner and commander approval. (3) Mission assurance: protect sensitive documents and patch Adobe/Java dependencies [S1]. (4) Coordination: Hungary's national security authority and CrySyS coordinated the original response, a model for partner-nation sharing [S4].
